## Introduction

[`targets`](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) is a package for R that manages a workflow in an R-native manner. It reduces the unnecessary rerunning of computationally heavy analyses after editing code, while ensuring that all affected downstream analyses are rerun. While other workflow managers such as Nextflow are more established and robust, I find them quite clunky to use while still developing the analysis. `targets` requires a restructuring of how your R code is written, but automatically keeps track of the components in your pipeline on a much more detailed level.

`targets` keep track of input files, intermediate R objects, functions and reports using hashes. It builds a pipeline using the file `_targets.R`, which is the primary file for editing your workflow. In this file, *targets* are defined as individual commands, and the dependency between commands are evaluated when the pipeline is visualised or run. Individual *targets* are saved and metadata is written to enable tracking whether they have changed since the last run.

## Demo repository

I have made a repository for use during the RSE tech group presentation. It can be cloned for testing `targets` on your own computer. The demo is performed using a Docker container which is available at jenfransson/rse_targets:latest and was built using the files in the repository.

<https://github.com/jenfransson/rse_targets/>

The repository contains two directories:

* `demo` : A nearly empty directory with instructions on how to get started
* `sc_example` : A directory with a more complicated pipeline. It illustrates a very simple scenario in which a scRNA-seq dataset needs to be filtered and processed. It contains examples of functions, branching and reports.


## Installation

### Installation with pixi (written by Claude, verified)

Install R and the packages with [Pixi](https://pixi.prefix.dev/).

```{.bash}
pixi init targets-demo
cd targets-demo
pixi add r-base r-targets r-tarchetypes r-crew r-readr r-ggplot2 r-visnetwork
```

::: {.callout-note}
On `osx-arm64`, the conda-forge `r-base64url` package (a dependency of `targets`) ships without its compiled library, and loading `targets` fails with ``shared object ‘base64url.so’ not found``. Fix it with `install.packages("base64url")` in R. `linux-64` is unaffected.
:::


### Other options

`targets` can also be installed from CRAN (`install.packages("targets")`) or renv (`renv::install("targets")`). In the demo repository, I installed it using renv in the rocker/rstudio based on the repository's `renv.lock` file.


## Getting started

To create a new targets project, navigate to a new folder (or `demo` in the repository) and start R. Then run:

```{.r}
library(targets)
use_targets()
```

This creates a new file called `_targets.R`, which is the main home for your pipeline-generating code<sup>1</sup>. The one generated by this function contains example code as well as comments about how to edit it.

## `_targets.R`

`_targets.R` has four main parts:

* Normal R code
    * Load any packages that are required to read the pipeline (not to run it), including `targets`
    * Set any global R options
* `tar_option_set()`
    * Define options for targets, such as packages needed to run the targets' commands and parallel computing options
* `tar_source()`
    * Source all .R-scripts in R/ as well as any other specified files
* Target list
    * The file ends with a list of `tar_target()` calls or other similar functions
        * `tarchetypes` provides other useful target-defining functions such as `tar_quarto*` and `tar_render*`
    * This list defines all of the targets that will be considered when building the pipeline
    * Any target defined in this list can be accessed in other targets' commands
    * The order of the targets does not matter

## Testing and running the pipeline

`targets` includes functions to visualise and run the pipeline. This is done outside of the `_targets.R` file, such as in the console or another script.

### `tar_make()`

`tar_make()` is the function called to evaluate and run the pipeline. Once started, the pipeline will be constructed from `_targets.R` and all input files and dependencies will be checked. If the pipeline can be constructed without errors, all outdated targets will be regenerated. During the run, the progress will be printed, but the verbosity can be adjusted using the `reporter` parameter. 

Note: Whether a target should be rerun or not is finally evaluated once all upstream targets have been checked and rerun (if needed). This means that in a default run, if a target was rerun due to e.g. a change to the command but the final object has the same hash, the downstream targets will not be rerun.

### `tar_visnetwork()`

`tar_visnetwork()` is the main function that I use for checking the status of my pipeline. It generates a DAG, with each function and target coloured according to whether they are outdated or not, or if they have errored. This graph quickly becomes messy once you have a decent number of targets, but it is interactive so you can zoom and highlight individual targets.

## Example

```{.r}
# Load packages
library(targets)

# Set up targets
use_targets()

# Visualize pipeline
tar_visnetwork()

# Run pipeline
tar_make()

# Visualize pipeline
tar_visnetwork()

# Read the target "model"
tar_read(model)

# Load the target "data" and examine it
tar_load(data)
head(data)
```

Edit _targets.R as you wish and examine the results using `tar_visnetwork` and `tar_make`


## `targets` outputs

All *targets* defined with `tar_target()` are stored in `_targets/objects` after creation <sup>1</sup>. The format of the output can be defined in the `tar_target()` function but is RDS by default. In addition, metadata including the hash of the object is stored in `_targets/meta/meta`. Changing or removing the files or editing the corresponding metadata will cause the *target* to be considered outdated and force it to be rerun in the next run.


## Reports

.Rmd- and .qmd-files can be included in your pipeline by using the [`tarchetypes` package](https://docs.ropensci.org/tarchetypes/) and functions `tar_render*()` and `tar_quarto*()`. Include these functions in the target-defining list in `_targets.R` and provide the `path` to your .Rmd- or .qmd-file. In the reports, include `library(targets)` and use `tar_read()` and `tar_load()` to refer to targets defined in your pipeline. During `tar_make()`, the dependencies will be established and the reports will only be re-rendered if they are outdated. 

## Branching

Branches can be used to e.g. test different analysis parameters or run the same pipeline on multiple datasets separately. Branches can be created in a static or dynamic fashion (documentation [here](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/static.html) and [here](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/dynamic.html)).

I won't go into details here, but there is an example in the [repository's `sc_example` subdirectory](https://github.com/jenfransson/rse_targets/tree/main/sc_example) of how to define dynamic branches using `pattern = map(...)` and creating separate reports from the different branches using `tar_quarto_rep()`.


## Key takeaways

* `targets` keeps track of all steps and dependencies within a pipeline
* Each *target* is defined as a command with inputs
* By default, only outdated *targets* will be recreated during a run
